title: Agentic Engineering: Working With AI, Not Just Using It — Brendan O'Leary

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 94%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is on coding agents, their workflows, and how engineers collaborate with them in software development. Coding assistants is the core domain with developer platforms as the substrate these agents run on. Covers both development-phase workflows and production-grade agent-driven software development. Requires familiarity with AI coding tools, Git workflows, and engineering management but is accessible to working engineers. The content is a conference-style talk by Brendan O'Leary from the AI Engineer channel. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript by the speaker.

summary: Brendan O'Leary defines "agentic engineering" as the practice of working with AI coding agents rather than simply using them, arguing most engineers cannot articulate their actual AI workflow despite 90% adoption. He traces AI's evolution from line completion to autonomous agents by 2025-2026 that decompose tasks, modify files, run tests, and produce pull requests. He proposes treating AI agents as energetic, well-read, confidently wrong junior developers who lack judgment and business context, requiring engineers to direct work and provide proper context like managing junior engineers. Context engineering is identified as the top tactical skill, with problems including cost, quality degradation beyond ~50% context capacity, context poisoning, and negative patterns persisting. Solutions include persisting information outside the context window, selective inclusion, summarizing, and isolating work across parallel agents. He details the research-plan-implement workflow: a research phase using a constrained mode that can only chat and read files, producing an output document for human review; a planning phase creating explicit step-by-step instructions with scope boundaries, verification strategies, and test commands; and an implementation phase starting fresh with only the plan, keeping context minimal. He emphasizes that human time at research and planning phases is the highest-leverage use of time, citing Dex Horthy's observation that a bad line of research can produce hundreds of lines of bad code, and that AI can't replace thinking—it only amplifies thinking done or exposes thinking not done. He covers agent configuration through three buckets: modes, agents.md, and skills.md. MCP servers extend agent capabilities but add context load, so unused MCPs should be disabled to avoid wasted tokens and agent confusion. For internal platform APIs, he recommends four approaches: using existing OpenAPI/Swagger specs, converting specs to markdown in agents.md, using reference URLs for frequently changing APIs, or building custom MCP servers for complex multi-system workflows. He stresses isolating agent work from human work and reviewing agent output as a pull request, just as one would review a junior engineer's code. He concludes by encouraging engineers to pick a tool, get lots of repetitions to develop a feel for what models can and cannot be trusted to do, try the research-plan-implement feedback loop, and notes that senior engineers report having more fun programming by offloading tedious work to agents while focusing on harder engineering problems.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: The Gap Between Using AI and Articulating Your Workflow
sections.summary: O'Leary opens by asking whether engineers can truly explain their AI workflow, noting 90% use AI tools but most cannot articulate how they decide what to hand off versus keep. This gap between usage and understanding defines the talk's focus.

sections.title: Evolution of AI in Software Engineering
sections.summary: Traces AI's rapid evolution from line completion (early 2020s) to function suggestion (2022, GitHub Copilot) to autonomous agents (2025-2026) that execute multi-step tasks and produce pull requests. Cites Armin Ronacher's framing that we now work with machines, not just use them.

sections.title: Mental Model: AI as Junior Developer
sections.summary: Proposes treating AI agents as energetic, well-read, confidently wrong junior developers who lack judgment and business context. Emphasizes that engineers must direct work and decide what to hand off, citing Armin's 30% time savings from knowing what to delegate.

sections.title: Context Engineering as the Critical Skill
sections.summary: Introduces context engineering via Karpathy's definition. Explains context is expensive (tokens re-sent as input), quality degrades beyond ~50% capacity, MCP servers add context load, and bad context from mixed tasks or outdated comments can poison output.

sections.title: Practical Context Management Techniques
sections.summary: Details four techniques: persist information outside context (scratchpads, memory files, agents.md), selectively include only relevant context, summarize and trim as context grows, and isolate work across parallel agents. Compares these to managing junior engineers.

sections.title: Balsamiq Intern Story and Habits for Success
sections.summary: Shares a story about interns building a prototype with Comic Sans fonts from a wireframe spec, illustrating that poor outcomes reflect the manager's failure to provide context. Recommends one task per session, monitoring context meter, and starting fresh sessions when off track.

sections.title: Research-Plan-Implement Workflow Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces the research-plan-implement workflow as a simpler, effective pattern. Notes most people jump straight to implementation requests, which leads to common mistakes. References path.kilo.ai for compiled workflow patterns.

sections.title: Research Phase: Understanding the Problem First
sections.summary: Explains that jumping straight to code causes wrong assumptions and frustration, creating anti-AI sentiment. The research phase uses a constrained mode (Kilo's ask mode) that can only chat and read files, not write code. It focuses on understanding the system, finding relevant files, identifying paradigms, mapping data flow, and brainstorming edge cases. The output is a research document for human review before proceeding to planning.

sections.title: Planning Phase: Explicit Steps and Scope
sections.summary: After reviewing research, the planning phase outlines specific files to create or change, verification strategies, test changes, and explicit in-scope and out-of-scope boundaries. The output is a clear plan file with step-by-step instructions and test commands. This allows potentially using a smaller, faster, or cheaper model for implementation since the thinking is done.

sections.title: Implementation Phase and Git as Local Review
sections.summary: Implementation starts in a fresh session with only the plan, keeping context minimal. Enables careful review of each change and frequent commits. O'Leary uses Git locally as his first pull request review before submitting to colleagues. Emphasizes human time at research and planning is the highest-leverage use of time, citing Dex Horthy that AI can't replace thinking, only amplify it or expose its absence.

sections.title: Agent Configuration: Modes, agents.md, and skills.md
sections.summary: Describes three configuration buckets: modes (role-based behaviors like ask, code, architect), agents.md (always-on project rules, conventions, build/test commands becoming a de facto standard), and skills.md (on-demand reusable playbooks for specific workflows like changelog compilation). Also covers tuning agent behavior: parallel agents, work trees, auto-approve settings, and tool permissions.

sections.title: Power User Tips and MCP for Extended Context
sections.summary: Covers at-mentioning files/commits/terminal output for quick context, slash commands for new tasks and context condensing, VS Code code selection for targeted questions, autocomplete in prompts, and using agents across CLI, mobile, cloud, and Slack. Introduces MCP servers as a way to extend agent capabilities with external tools like GitHub API access and context7 for up-to-date framework documentation beyond LLM knowledge cutoffs.

sections.title: MCP Management, Internal APIs, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Warns that every MCP server adds tokens to the system prompt, so unused MCPs should be disabled to avoid wasted tokens and agent confusion (e.g., a Postgres MCP during front-end work). For internal platform APIs, recommends four approaches: use existing OpenAPI/Swagger specs, convert to markdown in agents.md, use reference URLs for frequently changing APIs, or build custom MCP servers for complex multi-system workflows. Stresses isolating agent work and reviewing it as a pull request. Concludes by encouraging engineers to pick a tool, get many repetitions, try the research-plan-implement loop, and notes senior engineers report renewed enjoyment programming after offloading tedious work to agents. Mentions Kilo Code's upcoming features including OpenClaw safety and invites feedback at kilo.ai.
